transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, I came because... at church, you know, they have the potluck, and I always liked helping with the napkins and all that. My mother used to fold napkins real neat, corners matched, and I still think about that sometimes. But lately I do strange things there. I’ll be standing by the food table holding the serving spoon up and just not moving, or I keep folding the same little stack of napkins over and over while folks are waiting on me. It’s embarrassing.
Do you feel anxious or have a sense of panic when you find yourself doing these repetitive actions at church?

I don’t know if I’d call it panic, doctor. I mean, I get embarrassed when people are waiting, and then I think about whether the table looks right, and the napkins—my mother always said a crooked napkin made the whole place look untidy. But anxious? I’m not sure. It’s more like I get stuck there, and then afterward I feel foolish.

Do you have thoughts that come into your mind that you don’t want or welcome, and do you feel like you have to do these things with the napkins or the serving spoon to make those thoughts go away or to keep something bad from happening?

I don’t know, doctor… I don’t rightly notice a thought like that, like “do this or something bad will happen.” It’s not like when my aunt used to say you had to throw salt over your shoulder—she was always doing little things like that in the kitchen. With me, I just sort of get caught up with the napkins or the spoon, and then I realize people are looking. I’m not sure what I’m trying to make go away.
Do you ever have thoughts that come into your mind that you don’t want or find disturbing, even if you don’t act on them?

I’m not sure, doctor. I mean, everybody has odd thoughts, don’t they? Like I’ll be sitting there and remember I forgot to rinse a cup, or I’ll think about my neighbor’s curtains because she changed them last spring and they were too bright, in my opinion. But disturbing thoughts… I don’t know that I’d call them that. I don’t really notice something like that coming in and bothering me on its own.

Doctor: Do you ever feel like you have to do something, like folding the napkins a certain way or holding the spoon just right, because not doing it that way might lead to something bad happening, even if it doesn’t make much sense?

I don’t know that it’s like that, doctor. I don’t sit there thinking, “Oh, if I don’t hold the spoon this way something awful will happen.” It’s more… well, the spoon looks better turned a certain way, you know? My sister used to fuss at the table settings at holidays, and once she had all the forks wrong and everybody talked about it for weeks. But no, I can’t say I notice a bad thing I’m trying to stop. I just get fixed on it somehow.
Doctor: Do you ever have sudden, unwanted impulses or mental images that upset you or make you feel very uncomfortable, even if you don’t talk about them or act on them?

Sudden images… I don’t know, doctor. I can’t say I’ve noticed anything like that jumping into my head and upsetting me. Sometimes I’ll picture things from years ago, like my mother’s old kitchen curtains or the way the table looked at Christmas, but that’s just memory, isn’t it? Not something awful I’m trying not to think. I’m not sure I understand exactly what kind of images you mean.
Are there ever thoughts that come to you that you actively try not to think about, even if they’re not about something that most people would consider normal or reasonable?

I don’t think so, doctor. I mean, sometimes I try not to think about bills or whether I left something in the kitchen, but that’s just regular worries, isn’t it? Like this morning I was thinking about the blue dish towel, the one with the little flowers, because I couldn’t remember where I put it, and then I got thinking about my aunt’s towels, she always kept them folded so sharp…

But no, I can’t say there are thoughts I’m fighting off like that. I haven’t really noticed that happening.
Do you feel upset or anxious if someone interrupts you while you’re folding the napkins or adjusting the spoon, or if you’re not able to finish the way you want to do it?

I don’t know if it’s anxious exactly… I get kind of stuck. Like at church, that’s part of why I came, because I’ll be by the potluck table and I’ll just stand there holding the serving spoon up, not moving, while people are trying to get past me. Or I’ll fold the same stack of napkins over and over, and someone will say, “Are those ready?” and then I feel all mixed up, like I can’t get myself to stop right. 

It’s embarrassing, because people are waiting, and then I start thinking about how my mother used to want the napkins just so, but that’s not really what you asked. I just… yes, if I can’t finish it the way it feels it ought to be, I get bothered.
Do these kinds of behaviors or thoughts ever happen when you're at home or doing other things, or is it only when you're at church helping with the potluck?

Well… it’s mostly the church that I came about, doctor. The potluck table, you know, with everyone standing there with plates, and I’ll be holding the serving spoon up like I’m about to scoop something and then I just don’t move. Or I’ll keep folding the same napkins, over and over, while people are waiting.

At home I don’t know if I’d notice it the same way, because there aren’t people behind me saying, “Come on now.” I straighten little things sometimes, but the embarrassing part, the odd part, is really when I’m helping at church and I get stuck there.
Do these behaviors or thoughts ever cause you distress or interfere with your daily life when you're not at church, like at home or in other situations?

Well… not so much at home like the spoons and napkins, I guess, but it has gotten in the way some. I had to stop doing a few things with choir and helping at church, because I’d mix up who was supposed to do what, or what plan we had talked about. Then people would get awkward, or they’d have to fix it after me.

I used to like helping, you know. I remember when we had the old hymn books, the red ones, and we’d stack them after practice… but now I don’t always keep things straight, and it makes folks uncomfortable. So I’ve stepped back some.
Outside of church activities, do you ever feel upset, frustrated, or distressed because of these behaviors or thoughts—even if it’s just at home when no one is watching?

I’m not sure, doctor. At home it’s quieter, so I don’t notice it the same way. I might fiddle with things a bit, but I don’t know that I get upset like at church.

Sometimes I’ll start thinking about the cupboard or the towels, and then I remember my sister used to fold towels with the little edge showing—she said it looked nicer that way. But no one’s waiting on me at home, so it’s hard to say if it’s distressing. I mostly just… do it and move on, I think.
Outside of church, do you ever feel that these thoughts or behaviors interfere with things you need to do at home, like chores, errands, or other responsibilities?

At home… I mean, the dishes get done sooner or later, and I don’t have a job to get to now. So it’s not quite the same.

The bigger trouble has been with the church things, like choir and volunteering. I’ve had to step back from some of that because I get mixed up about what plan we made, or who was supposed to do which part, and then people sort of look at me funny or they have to redo what I was meant to handle. I don’t like that feeling.

At home, I suppose it’s slower, but nobody’s waiting on me with a casserole dish in their hands, you know.
Do you ever feel frustrated or upset because you can’t stop thinking about certain things or completing certain actions, even when you’re alone at home?

I don’t know if I’d say frustrated, exactly. When I’m alone, I just sort of do what I’m doing, and then it passes.

Sometimes I’ll get caught up with something small, like how a thing is sitting on the table, and then I think of my mother’s kitchen table—she had this oilcloth with little yellow flowers on it, and we weren’t supposed to put hot pans down. But… no, I don’t know that I’m upset about it. It’s more like I notice it, fiddle with it, and then go on.
Even when you're alone at home, do you ever feel that these thoughts or actions interfere with your ability to get things done or make you feel upset, even a little?

At home, it’s… I don’t know, it’s not as clear. I can get things done eventually. But I guess the place it really shows is church.

I’ve had to step back from some choir things and the volunteering because I mix up what we planned, or who was doing what, and then people get uneasy or they have to redo the part I was supposed to handle. That does bother me. I don’t like feeling like I’m making extra work for folks.
Even if you're not at church, do you ever feel that these thoughts or behaviors make it hard for you to do things you need to do or make you feel upset, even a little?

Well… away from church, I can putter around and it doesn’t show so much, I guess. The laundry waits, you know, it’s not like a person tapping their foot at you.

But I do get upset some, because with the choir and the volunteering I had to back off. I’d mix up what we’d planned, or who was supposed to bring what or do which part, and then folks get uncomfortable, or they have to go back and fix what I was meant to handle. That’s the part that makes me feel bad. I don’t like being the reason somebody else has to redo things.
Do you ever feel upset, frustrated, or distressed because of these thoughts or behaviors in situations outside of church, even if it's just a little?

I don’t really know. Outside of church… I mean, I get annoyed if I misplace my scissors or if the cupboard door won’t stay shut, but that’s just ordinary, isn’t it?

Sometimes I start on one thing and then remember something else, like I’ll go to wipe the counter and think about the curtains my aunt had, those heavy ones that smelled like dust when the sun hit them… and then I’m standing there with the rag in my hand. But I wouldn’t say I’m distressed, no. Not really. It just happens, and then I keep going when I notice.
Do these thoughts or behaviors ever cause you noticeable distress or make it hard for you to function in other parts of your life, like socially, at home, or in other activities outside of church?

Mostly it’s the church things where it’s noticeable. I keep saying that, I know, but that’s where people are depending on me.

I had to stop doing some choir things and some of the volunteering, because I’d get mixed up about what we’d planned or who was meant to do what. Then someone would look uncomfortable, or they’d have to go back and redo the part I was supposed to handle. That bothers me.

At home, I sort of go around it, you know… things can wait. But when other people are involved, that’s when it makes it hard.
Do you ever feel noticeable distress or find that these thoughts or behaviors make it hard for you to do things you need to do, even when you're not involved in church activities?

Not so much when I’m just at home, I don’t think. I can leave something and come back to it, or sometimes I just wander into another little task… like when you mean to fold towels and then you notice a drawer sticking, and then there you are with the towels still sitting.

But where it really made things hard was with the choir and the church volunteering. I had to step back from some of that, because I was mixing up the plans, or who was supposed to do what, and then people would get uncomfortable or have to redo what I was meant to handle. That’s the part that bothers me.

I don’t know if I’d say frustrated, exactly. When I’m alone, I just sort of do what I’m doing, and then it passes.

Sometimes I’ll get caught up with something small, like how a thing is sitting on the table, and then I think of my mother’s kitchen table—she had this oilcloth with little yellow flowers on it, and we weren’t supposed to put hot pans down. But… no, I don’t know that I’m upset about it. It’s more like I notice it, fiddle with it, and then go on.

At home, it’s… I don’t know, it’s not as clear. I can get things done eventually. But I guess the place it really shows is church.

I’ve had to step back from some choir things and the volunteering because I mix up what we planned, or who was doing what, and then people get uneasy or they have to redo the part I was supposed to handle. That does bother me. I don’t like feeling like I’m making extra work for folks.

patient.answer:
Well… away from church, I can putter around and it doesn’t show so much, I guess. The laundry waits, you know, it’s not like a person tapping their foot at you.

But I do get upset some, because with the choir and the volunteering I had to back off. I’d mix up what we’d planned, or who was supposed to bring what or do which part, and then folks get uncomfortable, or they have to go back and fix what I was meant to handle. That’s the part that makes me feel bad. I don’t like being the reason somebody else has to redo things.

patient.answer:
I don’t really know. Outside of church… I mean, I get annoyed if I misplace my scissors or if the cupboard door won’t stay shut, but that’s just ordinary, isn’t it?

Sometimes I start on one thing and then remember something else, like I’ll go to wipe the counter and think about the curtains my aunt had, those heavy ones that smelled like dust when the sun hit them… and then I’m standing there with the rag in my hand. But I wouldn’t say I’m distressed, no. Not really. It just happens, and then I keep going when I notice.

patient.answer:
Mostly it’s the church things where it’s noticeable. I keep saying that, I know, but that’s where people are depending on me.

I had to stop doing some choir things and some of the volunteering, because I’d get mixed up about what we’d planned or who was meant to do what. Then someone would look uncomfortable, or they’d have to go back and redo the part I was supposed to handle. That bothers me.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits repetitive behaviors (e.g., repeatedly folding napkins, fixating on placement of a serving spoon) and difficulty shifting attention or stopping these behaviors once initiated, particularly in social settings like church. These behaviors are associated with mild distress and functional impairment in social and volunteer roles, but there is no clear evidence of intrusive, unwanted thoughts or a sense of compulsion to prevent a feared event. The behaviors appear more ritualistic and mildly impairing but lack the full constellation of obsessions and compulsions seen in more complex OCD subtypes.
